The invention is credited to Omrao Khan Beenkar and his disciple Ghulam Mohammad; others credit Ustad Sahebdad Khan, and recent research also suggests the Lucknow sitar player Ustad Ghulam Mohammed as a possible inventor. A similar instrument, the Mahakachhapi Vina, existed at the same time. The surbahar is a chordophone used in Hindustani classical music of the Indian subcontinent, close to the sitar but lower in range.

The surbahar is a plucked chordophone of North Indian classical music in South Asia, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.321-5, close to the sitar; depending on the size of the body it usually sits two to five whole tones below a standard sitar. The body is over a hundred and thirty centimetres long and uses a dried gourd as its resonator, the neck carries wide frets, and the strings can be pulled to make slides of up to an octave; there are three or four rhythm strings, four main strings and ten to eleven sympathetic strings, and two bridges produce the buzzing jawari timbre. The player plucks with a plectrum of curved steel wire, and in the dhrupad style uses three plectra to play the slow, rhythmic and fast sections, accompanied by the pakhawaj drum.

The source states that the body uses a dried gourd as the resonator, that the top is a carved wooden plate, and that the neck is of mahogany or of the toon wood the source names, with the neck and the body joined by a carved wooden joint. The plectrum is curved steel wire. The source does not state the materials of the remaining parts, such as the strings, the bridges and the top.
蘇巴哈爾琴音色深邃溫潤，帶有沉靜而神秘的氣質。其低沈音域較標準西塔琴降低2至5個: The surbahar's timbre is deep and warm, with a calm, mysterious air. Its low range sits 2 to 5 whole tones below a standard sitar, and the resonance is full and powerful. The sound the strings make is ample and embracing: it keeps a clear, metallic penetration while also carrying the warmth of a wooden resonator. Beside the bright elegance of the sitar the surbahar is more sober and inward; beside a bass guitar its tone has more of the subtle flavour and ornamental slides of Indian classical music. Its resonator design amplifies the low frequencies fully, so a note decays gradually in the resonance and leaves a long, reverberant sound.
